newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - Data signals no early South African rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Data signals no early South African rate cut.

text.p: A mixed batch of economic data on Wednesday signalled South Africa could expect no early cut in current high interest rates, officials and economists said.
Consumer price inflation climbed to a 22-month high of 9.9 percent in April, up from 9.6 percent in March, disappointing the market which had been banking on an unchanged rate.

At the same time the annual growth in private sector credit extension increased to 16.95 percent against 15.95 percent in March, indicating South Africans are still borrowing too much for the central Reserve Bank's liking.
There was some good news with year-on-year broadly defined M3 money supply growing only 15.44 percent in April from 16.46 in March.
But all in all, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said there was nothing in the figures to change his conservative stance on monetary policy.
"All three statistics confirm again that we still have to be very, very cautious with the policy," Stals told Reuters by telephone from Pretoria.
Nonethless, economists said South Africa could still be on course for a cut in interest rates later in the year.

"We continue to look for a rate cut later in the third quarter and (the data) help us to stick with that. It says things are slowing down an the economy and we expect these money supply figures to come off in the coming months which will then pave the way for some easing," said Rand Merchant Bank treasury economist Julia Roy.

The bond market refused to get excited after the money supply and credit figures, released at 1500 GMT. Long bond yields fell from a pre-data high of 15.06 percent to 15.02 percent but this was no better than Tuesday's late level of 14.98 percent.
BOE NatWest strategic economist Nick Barnardt said he took some comfort from the money supply data.
"It was a moderate monthly rise for bank credit and a slight fall in the level of M3 so on balance it's slightly bullish," he said.

But ABN Amro's Anastasia Gekis said the earlier CPI data was disappointing, especially since the market was looking to the April figure to provide a basis for a trend decline for the rest of the year.
"It...puts a bit of a damper on hopes for an interest rate cut. It probably delays it slightly, to near the end of the year," she said.

"We are not going to come down (cut rates) soon, certainly. But we will watch it very carefully. The trends in real economic activity certainly indicate a slowdown and one must expect that these financial areas must follow sooner or later," he said.
South Africa's official Bank rate is currently set at 17 percent while commercial banks' prime lending rate is 20.25 percent, a real interest rate of over 10 percent after allowing for inflation.
